title: Next-token Preference: Scaling Unsupervised Reward Modeling
claim: Raw text can be turned into preference pairs automatically by treating each prefix's true continuation as chosen and other continuations as rejected.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, text sources feeding a batch score matrix
description: The figure has two panels read left to right. The left panel, titled 'Math Web Text', stacks three grey text boxes with small icons: QA platform threads, concept tutorials and math papers. Below them is a bracket labeled 'chunk to sequences of length L'. The right panel, 'Online Preference Pairing', first shows two blue text snippets split into prefix and suffix. Below, a batch of B sequences is drawn as blue prefix boxes x1..xB beside light suffix boxes y1..yB. An arrow labeled 'All-to-all RM scoring' with S_ij = s_θ(x_i, y_j) leads to a B×B score matrix. Diagonal cells are green (chosen, same sequence) and off-diagonal cells are red (rejected, other sequences). A legend and the note '1 chosen vs. B−1 rejected' sit at the bottom. The eye goes first to the colored matrix.
caption: Schematic overview of our NTP reward model training workflow from web math text. Raw documents are split into prefix–suffix pairs, where the true continuation is treated as the chosen response and other in-batch continuations serve as implicit negatives. The reward model is trained with a Bradley–Terry objective over these online preference pairs, enabling scalable reward learning without human annotations.
abstract: Learning from feedback advances the capabilities and safety of frontier models, but preference supervision remains costly and difficult to scale. We introduce next-token preference (NTP), an unsupervised reward-modeling method that constructs preference pairs from the continuation structure of raw web text. NTP uses each prefix's original continuation as the chosen response and nearby continuations as in-batch negatives, without candidate generation or human or model-generated preference annotations. Training on 11M tokens of math-focused web data yields steady gains on RewardBench and RewardBench 2, with gains across model families and sizes. Across mathematical and general-domain web corpora, our method improves overall RewardBench 2 accuracy by 7.6-8.3 percentage points over initialization under the same token budget. Training on math-focused text yields gains of up to +16.1 on in-domain math subsets and consistent improvements on out-of-domain safety and general subsets. These reward models improve best-of-N selection on math, code, safety, and instruction following, and support math policy optimization competitive with supervised reward models of similar size. NTP also improves the label efficiency of subsequent supervised fine-tuning. Using half the labeled pairs from a curated preference dataset, NTP initialization surpasses base initialization trained on the full dataset. These results suggest that web text contains transferable preference signals that can reduce dependence on costly preference annotations.
